decision.explanation: The derivative of arcsec x is 1/(|x|√(x²−1)), and the integral of cos x is sin x. Thus f(x) = 2 arcsec x − 3 sin x + C.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x=\text{arcsec}\,x.
$$

Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x)=\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x-\int 3\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x-3\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\text{ arcsec }x-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Rewrite (x²−7)/(x²+1) as 1−8/(x²+1). Integrating term by term gives x−8 arctan x+C.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
This integral doesn't look like one of the basic ones. However, we can manipulate the numerator a bit  to make it look more like the denominator, which reveals a more familiar expression: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}-7}{{x}^{2}+1} & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1-1-7}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+1)-8}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{{x}^{2}+1}}{\cancel{{x}^{2}+1}}-\frac{8}{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =1-\frac{8}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Remembering that

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C,
$$

we can now calculate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (1-\frac{8}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x-\int \frac{8}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x-8\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x-8\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
